chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, who said: A sheikh from our Kufan companions narrated to me, saying:
'Isa ibn Shafaqiyya entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and he was a magician. People would come to him, and he would take payment for that.

So he said to him: 'May I be your ransom! I am a man whose profession was magic, and I used to take payment for that, and it was my livelihood. I have performed Hajj from it, and Allah favored me with meeting you, and I have repented to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So is there for me any way out regarding anything from that?'
He said, so Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Loosen it, and do not tie it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on earnings from magic if one repents?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) provides a nuanced legal ruling to 'Isa ibn Shafaqiyya, a professional magician who had accumulated wealth through his craft before repenting. The phrase 'loosen and do not tie' (ḥull wa lā taʿqid) signifies that his past earnings were considered pure (ṭayyib) and permissible to retain, as magic was not inherently invalidating of wealth in the same way as usury, provided he ceased the practice. This highlights the Shia scholarly distinction between the act itself and the purity of the resulting property, offering a practical precedent for those transitioning from a specific profession.
